title: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of a slow system: what was slow, what did you change, and what was the improvement?
shortTitle: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of a slow system: what was slow, what you changed, and the improvement
keyPoints: Always measure before changing anything : performance intuition is unreliable.
Quantify the slowness with a real metric such as p99 latency or SLA breach percentage.
Profile to find the real bottleneck rather than scattering micro-optimizations.
Fix the specific thing the profiler points to, then verify with before-and-after numbers.
Check that the fix did not break correctness : a faster wrong answer is worse than a slow right one.
State the improvement as a business-relevant number such as latency, throughput, or cost.
Mention any trade-off you accepted, such as slightly stale cached data, to keep the answer honest.

s1_definition.oneliner: Measure first, fix the real bottleneck, verify with before-and-after numbers : never optimize on a guess.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Measure-first discipline** – Always profile and quantify the slowness before changing anything, because intuition about performance is famously unreliable.
- **Targeted fix** – Change only the specific code path the profiler identifies as the bottleneck, not a scattershot of micro-optimizations.
- **Before-and-after proof** – Verify the improvement with the same metric you used to diagnose, producing a concrete number.
- **Correctness guard** – Confirm that the faster version still produces correct results, especially with money.
- **Honest trade-offs** – If the fix introduces a trade-off such as caching with stale data, state it.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine customers complaining that the loan-approval desk at National Bank of India is slow. A guesser hires more staff randomly. A professional first measures where the time goes : forms take two minutes, but the credit check takes twenty : then fixes the credit check specifically. The improvement is measured: approvals go from twenty-five minutes to seven. That measure-first, fix-the-bottleneck discipline is exactly what this question rewards.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The slow system I improved at National Bank of India was the account-statement screen that customers like Rajesh and Priya use daily. Customers were complaining that pulling up a statement took around three seconds, which breached our one-second latency target, and it was worst for customers with long transaction histories. I owned the fix. The first thing I did was measure rather than guess. I profiled the endpoint and the data was unambiguous: almost all the time was spent in the database, not in the application logic.

When I looked closer, it was a classic N+1 query problem. To build the statement, the code loaded the account and then fired a separate database query for every single transaction. For a customer with five hundred transactions, that was over five hundred round-trips to the database, and each round-trip has a cost that adds up quickly. The fix was targeted at exactly that bottleneck: instead of querying per transaction, I batched them into a single query that fetched all the transactions at once.

The improvement was dramatic and, importantly, measured. The p99 for that endpoint dropped from three thousand milliseconds to around one hundred and eighty, comfortably under our SLA. I verified the output was identical before and after, because a faster but wrong statement would be far worse than a slow correct one, especially with money.

The reason I tell it this way is that performance work lives or dies on discipline. I always measure before I change anything, because intuition about performance is unreliable and it is easy to waste days optimizing code that was never the bottleneck. I fix the specific thing the profiler points to, verify with real before-and-after numbers, and I am honest about any trade-off.

Remember one sentence: Measure first, fix the real bottleneck the profiler shows you, and prove the improvement with before-and-after numbers.
